Changers
chānj'ers
n. pl. (money-changers; the temple exchange whose tables the Lord overthrew)
From change, Latin cambiare, to barter. The Greek in John 2:14 is kermatistes, a dealer in small coin, and in verse 15 kollubistes, from the kollubos or exchange fee — the commission is built into the name.

Biblical Definition

“And found in the temple those that sold oxen and sheep and doves, and the changers of money sitting” (John 2:14). Their trade was necessary in itself: pilgrims arrived with foreign coin bearing pagan images, and the temple tax had to be paid in acceptable currency. The offence was the place and the profit. “And when he had made a scourge of small cords, he drove them all out of the temple, and the sheep, and the oxen; and poured out the changers' money, and overthrew the tables” (John 2:15). His stated charge is not fraud but commerce: “Take these things hence; make not my Father's house an house of merchandise” (John 2:16). At the second cleansing, near the end of His ministry, Matthew records that He “overthrew the tables of the moneychangers, and the seats of them that sold doves” (Matthew 21:12), and there He quotes Isaiah and Jeremiah — a house of prayer made a den of thieves. The doves matter: they were the offering of the poor, and the poor were paying a markup to worship. The scourge was made by hand, of small cords, which means it was made deliberately and not in a moment's temper.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a changer as one that changes, and a money-changer as a broker who deals in the exchange of money.

expand to see more

CHANGER, n. One that alters the form of any thing.

2. One that is employed in changing and discounting money; a money-changer.

EXCHANGE, n. The act of giving one thing or commodity for another.

MERCHANDISE, n. The objects of commerce; wares, goods, commodities, whatever is usually bought or sold in trade.

TABLE, n. A frame or board on which money is counted; the counter of a money-changer.

Key Scripture

John 2:14 — "And found in the temple those that sold oxen and sheep and doves, and the changers of money sitting:"

John 2:15 — "And when he had made a scourge of small cords, he drove them all out of the temple, and the sheep, and the oxen; and poured out the changers' money, and overthrew the tables;"

John 2:16 — "And said unto them that sold doves, Take these things hence; make not my Father's house an house of merchandise."

Matthew 21:12 — "And Jesus went into the temple of God, and cast out all them that sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the tables of the moneychangers, and the seats of them that sold doves,"

Modern Corruption

The cleansing is quoted against every commercial abuse except the one it names — selling access to worship, especially to the poor.

expand to see more

The episode is a favourite text for sermons against greed in general, and its actual target is narrower and closer to home: a religious establishment monetising access to the worship of God. The changers were not con men operating outside the system; they were licensed, necessary, and inside the temple precincts, and the doves they sold were the offering the law appointed for those who could not afford a lamb. That is the arrangement Christ overturned with a scourge He took the time to make. Any ministry that puts a price between a poor worshipper and the God he came to worship — a conference fee, a course, a giving level attached to standing — is standing at the changers' table, whatever its accounting is like.

The second misuse is the appeal to this passage to justify anger, as though the scene licensed the sharp temper a man has already decided to indulge. Note the details John supplies. The scourge was made of small cords, by hand, which takes time; the doves were told to be taken out rather than released, since driving them off would have destroyed the property of men who were not the principal offenders; and the charge given is a sentence of doctrine, not an insult. This is judicial action by the Son in His Father's house, not a loss of composure, and the man who cites it for his own outbursts has borrowed the wrong precedent.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kermatistes (G2773), a money-changer — John 2:14, its only occurrence; kollubistes (G2855), an exchanger — John 2:15, Matthew 21:12, Mark 11:15; emporion (G1712), a house of merchandise — John 2:16.

expand to see more

Greek kermatistes (G2773) — a dealer in small change; John 2:14, its only occurrence in the New Testament.

Greek kollubistes (G2855) — an exchanger, named from the kollubos or commission; John 2:15, Matthew 21:12, Mark 11:15.

Greek emporion (G1712) — a place of merchandise, a market; John 2:16, its only occurrence.

Greek phragellion (G5416) — a scourge of cords; John 2:15, its only occurrence, and made by hand.

John 2:17 records the disciples' recollection: the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up.

Usage

"“Poured out the changers' money, and overthrew the tables” — the trade was licensed and inside the precincts."

"“Make not my Father's house an house of merchandise” — the charge is commerce, not fraud."

"The scourge was made of small cords, which takes time."
